content: Is there code for anything related to automorphism towers of groups or Wielandt's theorem, I was thinking of doing my bachelor's thesis on this. Specifically, the automorphism tower of a finite centreless group terminates after finitely many steps. (Automorphism tower meaning taking the automorphism group of a group, the automorphism group of that group and so on).

My suspicion is that this is a quite ambitious bachelor's thesis. (I'd need much more context on your background / advisor's background to advise.)

We'd need generalized Fitting subgroups, Bender's theorem about them, the three subgroups lemma, ... I think none of these are in Mathlib yet. It would be great to get them all in!
(btw, maybe you've already seen this, but https://site.uvm.edu/rfoote/files/2025/11/Wielandt-theorem-on-automorphism-towers.pdf seems a nice source)

Kim Morrison said:

the three subgroups lemma

docs#Subgroup.commutator_commutator_eq_bot_of_rotate

Maybe its ambitious but I'd like to try anyway, and even if I don't finish its likely I'll do some useful or interesting things (such as what you mentioned). I have a little experience with Lean, I've done all of MIL, I have used the group library a bit to show when the unit groups of integers mod n are cyclic and prove Iwasawa's criterion (I was aware these were done already when I wrote the code for them, I just wanted to practice). Right now I'm doing an 8 week project but its only on rings and combinatorics. My supervisor will likely have no experience with Lean.

Also thank you for sharing the source, I've been using Robinson which seems to prove this differently.

The ambition may not lie where you think, in terms of some sort of intellectual threshold, it is rather your time investment.

Without a lot of prior Lean experience it’s really easy to underestimate the ‘difficulty’ of proving things that seem fine on paper.

You may soon run into a descending chain of implications via citations in various levels of rigour that you must first formalise too, up to whatever is already there ( as mentioned above ).

If you have the time to commit to it , and the interest to learn, I don’t doubt you will eventually be able to do it ( here you may be constrained by bachelor duration / whatever deadlines you may have ) :smiling_face:

FWIW I've got extensive experience with supervising bachelor's projects and when people come along and say "I want to do X for my project" I never say "doing X is impossible in that time frame", instead I say "that's a great idea, let's start with X in mind and see how far we get".

I would just go for it. This isn't mathlib so you don't have to make the proof sorry-free. If you realise that you want to prove X but need Y and don't have enough time for everything then just choose whether to prove X assuming Y or to prove Y instead. As long as you're learning, and doing, then you're writing a bachelor's project.
